nodes.title: A1. Piece Rate (Lazear 2000, Safelite)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Layer output-contingent slope on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = \alpha + \beta\, s_i, \quad s_i = g(e_i) + \varepsilon_i$$

Worker's problem (CARA-Gaussian):
$$\max_{e_i}\; \alpha + \beta g(e_i) - c(e_i) - \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\beta^2\sigma^2$$

FOC: $\beta\, g'(e_i^{*}) = c'(e_i^{*}) \Rightarrow e_i^{*} > 0$.

Optimal slope (Holmström–Milgrom 1987):
$$\beta^{*} = \frac{1}{1 + \rho\,\sigma^2\, k/g'^{\,2}}$$

Efficiency loss vs first-best: $\Delta = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\sigma^2(\beta^{*})^2$.

---

**Signal**: individual measured output.

**Solves**
- Connects worker utility to firm output.
- Strong effort incentive.
- Sorts high-productivity types into the firm (Safelite: ~half the 44% gain is sorting).

**Breaks**
- Measurement error → risk transfer.
- Multitasking (Holmström–Milgrom 1991).
- Ratchet (Gibbons 1987).
- Goodhart / bunching.
- Cooperation collapse (Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003).

**Use when**: output perfectly measurable, quality clearly enforceable, production individual (Safelite is the textbook case).

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. (2000)**. Performance pay and productivity. *AER*, 90(5), 1346–1361 (Safelite study, 44% productivity gain).
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity in the provision of intertemporal incentives. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328 (optimal linear contract).
- **Holmström, B. (1979)**. Moral hazard and observability. *Bell JE*, 10, 74–91 (canonical PA setup).
- **Grossman, S. & Hart, O. (1983)**. An analysis of the principal-agent problem. *Econometrica*, 51(1), 7–45.
- **Mirrlees, J. (1975)**. The theory of moral hazard and unobservable behaviour. Working paper (later 1999 REStud).
- **Ross, S. (1973)**. The economic theory of agency: the principal's problem. *AER Papers & Proceedings*, 63(2), 134–139.

nodes.title: A2. Tournament / Rank-Order Contest (Lazear–Rosen 1981)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Replace flat $w_0$ with rank-based prizes: winner gets $w_H$, loser $w_L$, spread $\Delta = w_H - w_L$. $P_i(\text{win})$ depends on relative effort.

Worker's problem:
$$\max_{e_i}\; \Delta \cdot P_i(\text{win} \mid e_i, e_{-i}) - c(e_i)$$

Lazear–Rosen (1981) optimal spread:
$$\Delta^{*} \cdot \frac{\partial P_i}{\partial e_i} = c'(e_i^{*})$$

Common noise $\varepsilon$ cancels — only *relative* effort determines rank.

---

**Signal**: your *rank* among peers, not your level.

**Solves**
- Cancels common shocks (market, weather, task difficulty) via relative comparison → attacks F1 (measurement).
- Fights the ratchet (F3): can't hide capacity if effort still moves rank.
- Simple prize structure; only ordinal ranking needed.

**Breaks**
- Sabotage (Chan 1996; Dye 1984; Lazear 1989).
- Collusion: everyone agrees to low effort.
- Kills cooperation completely — helping a peer is directly costly (worsens F5).
- Discourages risky innovation late in the round if ahead.

**Use when**: individual output measurable up to a common shock, peer group homogeneous, cooperation not required.

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. & Rosen, S. (1981)**. Rank-order tournaments as optimum labor contracts. *JPE*, 89(5), 841–864.
- **Green, J. & Stokey, N. (1983)**. A comparison of tournaments and contracts. *JPE*, 91(3), 349–364 (common-shock cancellation).
- **Nalebuff, B. & Stiglitz, J. (1983)**. Prizes and incentives: towards a general theory of compensation and competition. *Bell JE*, 14(1), 21–43.
- **Chan, W. (1996)**. External recruitment versus internal promotion. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 14(4), 555–570 (sabotage).
- **Dye, R. (1984)**. The trouble with tournaments. *Economic Inquiry*, 22(1), 147–149 (sabotage).
- **Lazear, E. (1989)**. Pay equality and industrial politics. *JPE*, 97(3), 561–580 (sabotage/collusion).
- **Ehrenberg, R. & Bognanno, M. (1990)**. Do tournaments have incentive effects? *JPE*, 98(6), 1307–1324 (evidence).

nodes.title: A3. Fixed Wage + Efficiency Wage (Shapiro–Stiglitz 1984)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Keep $w_0 > w^{MC}$ (as in Weiss) **plus** monitoring probability $q$ + dismissal on detected shirking.

**Shapiro–Stiglitz no-shirking condition**:
$$w_0 - w^{MC} \;\geq\; \frac{c(e)\,(1-\delta)}{q\,\delta}$$

Wage premium must exceed effort cost adjusted by monitoring intensity. $e_i^{*} > 0$ induced by threat of losing the rent — not by output linkage.

---

**Signal**: none directly — pay is flat. Motivation from *threat of dismissal* under monitoring, plus wage above market-clearing so the job is worth keeping.

**Solves**
- Removes all output-based risk (F4).
- No metric to game → attacks multitasking (F2), Goodhart (F6).
- No incentive to hoard output → attacks cooperation collapse (F5).

**Breaks**
- Requires credible monitoring AND credible dismissal.
- Involuntary unemployment as equilibrium feature.
- No high-powered incentive → productivity ceiling.

**Use when**: output signals noisy or gameable; quality > quantity; firm has monitoring infrastructure.

---

### References

- **Shapiro, C. & Stiglitz, J. (1984)**. Equilibrium unemployment as a worker discipline device. *AER*, 74(3), 433–444.
- **Yellen, J. (1984)**. Efficiency wage models of unemployment. *AER Papers & Proceedings*, 74(2), 200–205 (survey).
- **Salop, S. (1979)**. A model of the natural rate of unemployment. *AER*, 69(1), 117–125 (turnover-cost variant).
- **Akerlof, G. (1982)**. Labor contracts as partial gift exchange. *QJE*, 97(4), 543–569.
- **Bulow, J. & Summers, L. (1986)**. A theory of dual labor markets. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 4(3), 376–414.
- **Krueger, A. & Summers, L. (1988)**. Efficiency wages and the inter-industry wage structure. *Econometrica*, 56(2), 259–293 (evidence).

nodes.title: A4. Team Pay / Profit Sharing (Kandel–Lazear 1992; Weitzman–Kruse 1990)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Add group-signal slope on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = w_0 + \beta_T \cdot s_{\text{team}}, \quad s_{\text{team}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N y_j$$

Marginal own-effort incentive:
$$\frac{\partial w_i}{\partial e_i} = \frac{\beta_T}{N}$$

Free-rider scales with $N$: individual reward on own effort $\propto 1/N$.

Kandel–Lazear (1992): peer pressure supplements the $1/N$ direct incentive for small $N$ — worker $i$ internalizes some cost of others' scrutiny.

---

**Signal**: group-level output — team quota, plant profits, firm profit.

**Solves**
- Rewards cooperation, mentoring, mutual help directly (F5).
- Aligns worker to firm value → attacks narrow-metric multitasking (F2).
- Peer pressure polices free-riders in small teams (Kandel–Lazear).

**Breaks**
- Free-rider problem grows with N — marginal reward on effort ≈ 1/N.
- Requires observability *between* peers so social pressure operates.
- Loads systematic risk (firm-wide shocks) onto workers — WORSENS F4.

**Use when**: small tight teams with strong cooperation externalities and mutual observability (surgical team, small startup).

---

### References

- **Kandel, E. & Lazear, E. (1992)**. Peer pressure and partnerships. *JPE*, 100(4), 801–817.
- **Weitzman, M. & Kruse, D. (1990)**. Profit sharing and productivity. In *Paying for Productivity*, Brookings.
- **Alchian, A. & Demsetz, H. (1972)**. Production, information costs, and economic organization. *AER*, 62(5), 777–795.
- **Holmström, B. (1982)**. Moral hazard in teams. *Bell JE*, 13(2), 324–340 (free-rider theorem).
- **Hamilton, B., Nickerson, J. & Owan, H. (2003)**. Team incentives and worker heterogeneity. *JPE*, 111(3), 465–497.
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2013)**. Team incentives: evidence from a firm level experiment. *JEEA*, 11(5), 1079–1114.

nodes.title: A7. Subjective Evaluation + Bonus (MacLeod 2003; Baker–Gibbons–Murphy 1994)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Manager privately observes rating $m_i$ correlated with effort. Bonus $b(m_i)$ on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = w_0 + b(m_i)$$

Worker's effort FOC:
$$\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\partial b(m_i)}{\partial e_i}\right] = c'(e_i^{*})$$

Optimal $b^{*}$ (MacLeod 2003) balances effort inducement against **influence-activity** cost. Requires a **relational contract**: manager must credibly commit not to renege; reneging destroys the equilibrium.

---

**Signal**: manager's private assessment, converted to bonus/promotion.

**Solves**
- Manager can down-weight lucky outcomes and reward true effort → attacks measurement noise (F1).
- Rewards multi-dim performance → attacks multitasking (F2).
- Preserves flexibility to reward cooperation, culture, mentoring (F5).
- No explicit threshold → no bunching (F6).

**Breaks**
- Influence activities (Milgrom 1988): workers persuade the manager instead of producing.
- Favoritism, discrimination, arbitrary variation.
- Requires a **relational contract**: manager must credibly commit to fair evaluation (MacLeod 2003).
- Legally hard to defend if evaluations diverge from measurables.

**Use when**: output is complex, multi-dimensional, hard to game via explicit metrics; long employment relationships with repeated interaction.

---

### References

- **MacLeod, W. B. (2003)**. Optimal contracting with subjective evaluation. *AER*, 93(1), 216–240.
- **Baker, G., Gibbons, R. & Murphy, K. J. (1994)**. Subjective performance measures in optimal incentive contracts. *QJE*, 109(4), 1125–1156.
- **Milgrom, P. (1988)**. Employment contracts, influence activities, and efficient organization design. *JPE*, 96(1), 42–60.
- **Prendergast, C. & Topel, R. (1996)**. Favoritism in organizations. *JPE*, 104(5), 958–978.
- **Levin, J. (2003)**. Relational incentive contracts. *AER*, 93(3), 835–857.
- **Prendergast, C. (2002)**. The tenuous trade-off between risk and incentives. *JPE*, 110(5), 1071–1102.

nodes.title: A8. Ownership / Equity (Hansmann 1996; Kruse–Blasi 1997)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

Add equity share $\phi \in (0,1)$ on top of $w_0$:
$$w_i = w_0 + \phi \cdot V, \qquad V = \sum_{j=1}^N y_j$$

Marginal own-effort incentive:
$$\frac{\partial w_i}{\partial e_i} = \phi \cdot \frac{\partial V}{\partial e_i}$$

For workforce size $N$, effective incentive per worker on own task is $\phi/N$ — free-rider like team pay. But alignment with **long-run** firm value handles multi-dim + horizon simultaneously.

---

**Signal**: firm value — worker holds a residual claim (stock, options, partnership share, ESOP).

**Solves**
- Aligns effort with long-run firm value → solves multitasking (F2) and horizon jointly.
- Rewards firm-level cooperation and mentoring (F5).
- Long horizon smooths short-run bunching (F6).
- Prices cooperation externality → useful when Safelite condition #3 (individual production) fails (F7).

**Breaks**
- Free-rider grows with N (each worker owns ≈ 1/N).
- Loads undiversified risk onto workers (labor income + wealth co-move) — WORSENS F4.
- Governance costs — worker-owners may block value-creating layoffs.
- Requires liquidity / vesting to prevent early cash-out.

**Use when**: small firm, high-skill workers, long horizon, output primarily reflects team effort (early-stage startup, law/consulting partnership).

---

### References

- **Hansmann, H. (1996)**. *The Ownership of Enterprise*. Harvard University Press.
- **Kruse, D. & Blasi, J. (1997)**. Employee ownership, employee attitudes, and firm performance. In *The Human Resources Management Handbook*.
- **Jensen, M. & Meckling, W. (1976)**. Theory of the firm: managerial behavior, agency costs and ownership structure. *JFE*, 3(4), 305–360.
- **Blasi, J., Kruse, D. & Freeman, R. (2018)**. Broad-based employee stock ownership and profit sharing. *Journal of Participation and Employee Ownership*, 1(1), 38–60.
- **Oyer, P. (2004)**. Why do firms use incentives that have no incentive effects? *Journal of Finance*, 59(4), 1619–1650.

nodes.title: A9. Selection-Based Pay Structure (Lazear 1986, 2000)
nodes.content:
### How this modifies the base model

**No modification.** Selection IS the base mechanism — Weiss (1980) + PVR (2002) already sort $\theta$ via $w_0$ and $w(z)$.

A9's contribution: makes the sorting margin *explicit* in contract design. The CHOICE of $(w_0, \{\beta_j\})$ operates through sorting as much as through moral hazard.

Lazear (2000): about **half** of Safelite's 44% productivity gain came from sorting, not effort. Selection is the silent workhorse layered underneath every other alternative.

---

**Signal**: the *contract itself* acts as a filter — the pay structure attracts one type and repels another.

**Solves**
- You don't need to motivate ex-post; you need to attract the right type ex-ante.
- Lazear (2000): ~**half** of the Safelite 44% productivity gain was *sorting*, not effort.
- Reduces monitoring cost — the contract does the screening.
- Complementary to any base scheme; layers on top.

**Breaks**
- Requires labor-market heterogeneity and mobility.
- Sorting alone is often insufficient; usually combined with incentives.
- Can create adverse selection if the signal the contract offers is misread.

**Use when**: heterogeneous labor market, type unobservable directly, you want a self-enforcing filter. Note: this changes WHO applies, not what workers do once hired — so it doesn't fix any specific failure, it prevents them from arising.

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. (1986)**. Salaries and piece rates. *Journal of Business*, 59(3), 405–431.
- **Lazear, E. (2000)**. Performance pay and productivity. *AER*, 90(5), 1346–1361 (empirical decomposition: sorting vs incentive at Safelite).
- **Weiss, A. (1980)**. Job queues and layoffs in labor markets with flexible wages. *JPE*, 88(3), 526–538 (sorting via wage level).
- **Salop, S. & Salop, J. (1976)**. Self-selection and turnover in the labor market. *QJE*, 90(4), 619–627 (back-loaded pay as sorting).
- **Guasch, J. L. & Weiss, A. (1981)**. Self-selection in the labor market. *AER*, 71(3), 275–284.

nodes.title: F1. Imperfect Performance Measurement
nodes.content:
**Problem**

The signal we contract on is $s = g(\text{effort}) + \varepsilon$, not effort itself. Any noise $\varepsilon$ in the measurement gets transmitted into the worker's pay.

**Consequences**
- Risk-averse workers demand a wage premium for bearing noise → higher wage bill.
- Or firm dampens piece rate to reduce risk exposure → weaker incentive → less effort.
- Either way, first-best not achievable (Holmström–Milgrom 1987 optimal linear contract: risk vs incentive intensity tradeoff).

**Which alternatives address it**
- A2 Tournament (cancels common shock)
- A6 Career concerns (market averages many signals)
- A7 Subjective (manager corrects for luck)

---

### References

- **Holmström, B. (1979)**. Moral hazard and observability. *Bell JE*, 10, 74–91.
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328.
- **Prendergast, C. (2002)**. The tenuous trade-off between risk and incentives. *JPE*, 110(5), 1071–1102.
- **Baker, G. (1992)**. Incentive contracts and performance measurement. *JPE*, 100(3), 598–614.

nodes.title: F2. Multitasking (Holmström–Milgrom 1991)
nodes.content:
**Problem**

If you reward one task among several, workers crowd out the un-rewarded tasks.

**Evidence**
- Asch (1990), Larkin (2014): piece rates on tasks A, B, C → worker picks only the mispriced (arbitrage) one.
- If firm tracks 3 tasks, worker finds the highest-marginal-return one and dumps the rest.

**Why**
Worker's cost of effort is convex; marginal reward differs across tasks. Optimal worker response is a corner solution unless firm equalizes marginal incentives across ALL relevant dimensions.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (no metric to game)
- A4 Team pay (broader signal)
- A6 Career concerns (market prices overall ability)
- A7 Subjective (rewards all dimensions)
- A8 Ownership (aligned to firm value)

---

### References

- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991)**. Multitask principal–agent analyses: incentive contracts, asset ownership, and job design. *JLEO*, 7(Special), 24–52.
- **Baker, G. (1992)**. Incentive contracts and performance measurement. *JPE*, 100(3), 598–614.
- **Asch, B. (1990)**. Do incentives matter? The case of Navy recruiters. *ILR Review*, 43(3), 89-S–106-S.
- **Larkin, I. (2014)**. The cost of high-powered incentives: employee gaming in enterprise software sales. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 32(2), 199–227.
- **Feltham, G. & Xie, J. (1994)**. Performance measure congruity and diversity in multi-task principal/agent relations. *Accounting Review*, 69(3), 429–453.

nodes.title: F3. Ratchet Effect (Gibbons 1987)
nodes.content:
**Problem**

Worker hides capacity — puts low effort in easy periods so the firm doesn't discover the task is easy and raise the quota next period. Roy (1952); Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2005).

**Mechanism**
Worker's optimal effort today depends on how effort maps to *tomorrow's target*, not just today's pay. High output today → tighter quota tomorrow → dampen output.

**Classical fix (Holmström 1982; Shleifer 1985)**
Index quota to *peers*, not own history — own effort no longer feeds own standard. Yardstick competition. This is essentially A2 Tournament.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A2 Tournament (peer-indexed quotas)
- A5 Deferred comp (long horizon dilutes ratchet gain)
- A6 Career concerns (market has no reason to raise your standard)

---

### References

- **Gibbons, R. (1987)**. Piece-rate incentive schemes. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 5(4), 413–429.
- **Roy, D. (1952)**. Quota restriction and goldbricking in a machine shop. *American Journal of Sociology*, 57(5), 427–442.
- **Weitzman, M. (1980)**. The 'ratchet principle' and performance incentives. *Bell JE*, 11(1), 302–308 (Soviet planning context).
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2007)**. Incentives for managers and inequality among workers: evidence from a firm-level experiment. *QJE*, 122(2), 729–773.
- **Holmström, B. (1982)**. Moral hazard in teams. *Bell JE*, 13(2), 324–340 (yardstick / peer benchmark).
- **Shleifer, A. (1985)**. A theory of yardstick competition. *RAND JE*, 16(3), 319–327.
- **Freixas, X., Guesnerie, R. & Tirole, J. (1985)**. Planning under incomplete information and the ratchet effect. *REStud*, 52(2), 173–191.

nodes.title: F4. Risk Transfer to Worker
nodes.content:
**Problem**

Pay = f(output). Output varies for reasons the worker cannot control: machine downtime, random customer arrivals, seasonal variation, task-difficulty heterogeneity.

**Consequence**
Risk-averse workers dislike income variance; they demand a risk premium. Firm pays MORE in expected wage bill for the same expected effort. The insurance-vs-incentive tradeoff (Holmström–Milgrom 1987) is the core of contract theory.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (removes ALL output risk)

**Which alternatives make it WORSE**
- A4 Team pay (loads systematic firm risk)
- A8 Ownership (undiversified: labor + wealth co-move)

---

### References

- **Ross, S. (1973)**. The economic theory of agency. *AER*, 63(2), 134–139.
- **Mirrlees, J. (1975/1999)**. The theory of moral hazard and unobservable behaviour. *REStud*, 66(1), 3–21.
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328 (risk-incentive tradeoff).
- **Prendergast, C. (2002)**. The tenuous trade-off between risk and incentives. *JPE*, 110(5), 1071–1102 (empirical test).
- **Ackerberg, D. & Botticini, M. (2002)**. Endogenous matching and the empirical determinants of contract form. *JPE*, 110(3), 564–591.

nodes.title: F5. Cooperation Collapse (Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003)
nodes.content:
**Evidence**
Garment plant switched from team pay to individual piece rates → total output FELL despite rising individual effort. Workers stopped teaching, helping, covering. Also Encinosa–Gaynor–Rebitzer (2007) on physician groups.

**Mechanism**
Under piece rates, time spent helping a peer = zero personal reward + opportunity cost of your own output. Rational response: withdraw from cooperation. Knowledge transfer disappears.

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (nothing to compete over)
- A4 Team pay (directly rewards cooperation)
- A7 Subjective (manager rewards mentoring)
- A8 Ownership (residual claim on joint output)

**Which alternatives make it WORSE**
- A2 Tournament (helping a peer is directly costly)

---

### References

- **Hamilton, B., Nickerson, J. & Owan, H. (2003)**. Team incentives and worker heterogeneity: garment plant evidence. *JPE*, 111(3), 465–497.
- **Encinosa, W., Gaynor, M. & Rebitzer, J. (2007)**. The sociology of groups and the economics of incentives. *JEBO*, 62(2), 187–214.
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2005)**. Social preferences and the response to incentives. *QJE*, 120(3), 917–962 (peer effects).
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2010)**. Social incentives in the workplace. *REStud*, 77(2), 417–458.
- **Freeman, R. & Medoff, J. (1984)**. *What Do Unions Do?* Basic Books (cooperation-through-voice).

nodes.title: F6. Goodhart / Bunching
nodes.content:
**Evidence**
- Oyer (1998): salespeople bunch deals before fiscal year-end.
- Larkin (2014): software sales *sandbag* large deals to avoid ratcheting next quarter.
- Camerer–Farber–Falk: taxi drivers, bike messengers stop at daily income target (backward-bending supply from loss aversion).

**Mechanism**
Any quota threshold creates a kink where marginal piece rate drops to zero (or turns negative via ratchet). Workers bunch AT the threshold — never above.

> "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure."

**Which alternatives address it**
- A3 Fixed wage (no threshold)
- A5 Deferred comp (long horizon smooths bunching)
- A6 Career concerns (continuous market pricing)
- A7 Subjective (no bright-line target)
- A8 Ownership (long-horizon claim)

---

### References

- **Goodhart, C. (1975)**. Problems of monetary management: the U.K. experience. Papers in Monetary Economics, Reserve Bank of Australia (origin of Goodhart's Law).
- **Oyer, P. (1998)**. Fiscal year ends and non-linear incentive contracts. *QJE*, 113(1), 149–185.
- **Larkin, I. (2014)**. The cost of high-powered incentives: employee gaming in enterprise software sales. *Journal of Labor Economics*, 32(2), 199–227.
- **Camerer, C., Babcock, L., Loewenstein, G. & Thaler, R. (1997)**. Labor supply of New York City cab drivers: one day at a time. *QJE*, 112(2), 407–441.
- **Farber, H. (2015)**. Why you can't find a taxi in the rain and other labor supply lessons from cab drivers. *QJE*, 130(4), 1975–2026.
- **Chevalier, J. & Ellison, G. (1997)**. Risk taking by mutual funds as a response to incentives. *JPE*, 105(6), 1167–1200 (kink-driven behavior).

nodes.title: F7. Safelite Preconditions (when piece rate works)
nodes.content:
**Three conditions that made Safelite work**

1. **Output perfectly measurable**: install-a-windshield-or-not; discrete, countable, homogeneous.
2. **Quality standard clear**: any leak/failure → worker returns to fix, unpaid, on own time. Solves the quality-quantity multitasking problem via ex-post penalty.
3. **Production individual**: no cooperation externalities to destroy. One worker, one car, one windshield.

**Implication for Quindi.AI**: violates #3 (cooperation matters) and possibly #1 (multi-dim AI-assisted output). Price cooperation, don't rely on a single scalar throughput.

---

### References

- **Lazear, E. (2000)**. Performance pay and productivity. *AER*, 90(5), 1346–1361 (Safelite study — the original documentation of the preconditions).
- **Paarsch, H. & Shearer, B. (1999)**. The response of worker effort to piece rates: evidence from the British Columbia tree-planting industry. *JHR*, 34(4), 643–667 (another individual, measurable, quality-easy-to-monitor setting).
- **Shearer, B. (2004)**. Piece rates, fixed wages and incentives: evidence from a field experiment. *REStud*, 71(2), 513–534.
- **Bandiera, O., Barankay, I. & Rasul, I. (2005)**. Social preferences and the response to incentives. *QJE*, 120(3), 917–962 (breakdown when preconditions fail).

nodes.title: ★ Agent-Based Model for Quindi
nodes.content:
# Agent-Based Model (ABM) for Quindi's Incentive Design

Simulate heterogeneous workers who under-produce for well-identified behavioral reasons, plug in each contract A0–A9 as a swappable module, and observe what happens to output, wage bill, cooperation, sabotage, and — crucially — the estimated $\hat\tau$ from the AI treatment.

---

# Part B — Behavioral mechanisms agents must embody

Each agent carries **attributes** (heterogeneous parameters) AND **behavioral rules** (how they respond to a contract).

## Agent attributes

| Symbol | Meaning | Distribution |
|---|---|---|
| $\varepsilon_i$ | Ability (efficiency units of labor) | $\sim H$, e.g. lognormal |
| $\rho_i$ | CARA risk aversion | $\sim$ truncated normal $(2, 1)$ |
| $k_i$ | Effort-cost curvature | $\sim$ gamma |
| $\phi_i$ | Reciprocity intensity (Akerlof–Fehr) | $\sim \text{Beta}(2, 2)$ |
| $\delta_i$ | Discount factor | $\sim U[0.90, 0.99]$ |
| $\mathcal{N}_i$ | Peer network (which workers $i$ observes) | Erdős–Rényi or small-world |
| $\bar w_i$ | Reference wage (last-period, peer avg) | Updated each period |
| $Y_i^{\text{target}}$ | Income target (loss aversion) | Set by peer earnings |

## Behavioral rules — why agents under-produce

Ten distinct mechanisms; each is a switchable component. Agents' effort $e_i$ is the equilibrium of these forces.

### 1. Shirking under flat wage (Shapiro–Stiglitz 1984)
$$\max_{e_i}\; w_0 - c(e_i) \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; e_i^{*} = 0$$

No monitoring → zero effort. Adds monitoring hazard $q$ + dismissal penalty $\Delta w$: worker exerts $e_i > 0$ iff $q\,\delta_i\,\Delta w \geq c(e_i)$.

### 2. Free-riding in teams (Alchian–Demsetz 1972; Holmström 1982; Kandel–Lazear 1992)
$$\frac{\partial w_i}{\partial e_i} = \frac{\beta_T}{n} \;\Rightarrow\; e_i^{*} \text{ decreasing in } n$$

Offset: peer pressure $\psi$ raises effective cost of shirking, $c(e_i) + \psi \cdot (\bar e_{\mathcal{N}_i} - e_i)^{+}$.

### 3. Multitasking arbitrage (Holmström–Milgrom 1991)
Worker allocates effort $\mathbf{e}$ across dims to equalise $\beta_j g_j'(e_j) = c_j'(e_j)$. If $\beta_j = 0$, worker sets $e_j = 0$ — crowd-out.

### 4. Ratchet strategic hiding (Gibbons 1987; Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul 2005)
If next-period target depends on this-period output:
$$e_{i,t}^{*} = e^{\text{one-shot}} - \alpha \cdot \frac{\partial \text{target}_{t+1}}{\partial s_{i,t}}$$

Worker under-produces to hide capacity.

### 5. Sabotage under tournaments (Chan 1996; Lazear 1989)
Worker chooses effort $e_i$ AND sabotage $\sigma_{ij}$ against peer $j$:
$$P_i(\text{win rank}) = P\big(g(e_i) - \textstyle\sum_j \sigma_{ji} > g(e_j) - \textstyle\sum_k \sigma_{kj}\big)$$

Optimum has $\sigma_{ij}^{*} > 0$ whenever the prize gap is large.

### 6. Loss-averse Goodhart bunching (Camerer–Babcock–Loewenstein–Thaler 1997; Kahneman–Tversky 1979)
$$U_i(w_i) = \begin{cases} w_i - Y_i^{\text{target}} & \text{if } w_i \geq Y_i^{\text{target}} \\ \lambda\,(w_i - Y_i^{\text{target}}) & \text{else},\; \lambda > 1 \end{cases}$$

Effort spikes just below target; drops sharply above → **bunching at kink**.

### 7. Reciprocity / gift exchange (Akerlof 1982; Fehr & Falk 2002)
$$e_i^{*} = e_i^{\text{base}} + \phi_i \cdot (w_i - \bar w_i)$$

Higher wage than reference → more effort even with $\beta = 0$. Adds a channel through which A3 (efficiency wage) works.

### 8. Peer effects / social conformity (Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul 2005, 2010; Mas & Moretti 2009)
Effort cost gets a peer-conformity term:
$$c(e_i) \;\to\; c(e_i) + \gamma \cdot (e_i - \bar e_{\mathcal{N}_i})^{2}$$

High-effort peers pull the worker up; low-effort peers drag them down.

### 9. Career-concern signalling (Holmström 1982; Gibbons–Murphy 1992)
Market Bayes-updates $\varepsilon_i$ from observed $s_t$; future wage $w_{t+1} = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i \mid s_1, \dots, s_t]$. Worker's effort FOC:
$$\delta_i \cdot \frac{\partial w_{t+1}}{\partial s_t} = c'(e_t^{*})$$

Declines toward retirement (horizon effect).

### 10. Cooperation externality collapse (Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan 2003; Encinosa–Gaynor–Rebitzer 2007)
Helping peer $j$ costs $h(a_{ij})$ but boosts $g_j$ by $\Delta g$:
- Under piece rate: help is unpaid → $a_{ij}^{*} = 0$.
- Under team pay / equity / subjective: help is (partially) priced → $a_{ij}^{*} > 0$.

---

# Part C — Simulation architecture

## 1. Population

- $N$ workers with attributes drawn from priors.
- $N/n$ teams of size $n$ (Quindi: $n = 5$).
- One firm of productivity $p$.

## 2. Contract module (plug-in interface)

Define an abstract interface:
```
class Contract:
    def wage(self, worker, signals, history): -> float
    def enter_period(self, workers): -> None    # e.g. tournament ranking
    def monitor(self, worker): -> bool          # for A3
```

Implementations:

| Contract | Implementation |
|---|---|
| **A0** Baseline | $w = w_0$ |
| **A1** Piece rate | $w = \alpha + \beta\, s_i$ |
| **A2** Tournament | $w = w_H$ if rank $\leq K$ else $w_L$ |
| **A3** Efficiency wage | $w = w_H$; monitoring prob $q$; dismiss if $s_i$ below threshold |
| **A4** Team pay | $w = \alpha + \beta_T\, \bar s_{\text{team}}$ |
| **A5** Deferred | $w_t = w_{\text{low}}$ if $t < T^{*}$; $w_t = w_{\text{high}}$ later |
| **A6** Career concerns | $w_{t+1} = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i \mid s_{1:t}]$ (market rule) |
| **A7** Subjective | $w = \alpha + b(m_i)$, $m_i = \varepsilon_i e_i + $ manager noise |
| **A8** Equity | $w = \alpha + \phi \cdot V_{\text{firm}}$ |

## 3. Time step (one period)

For $t = 1, 2, \dots, T$:

**(a)** *Contract announces state.* Enter_period hook runs (rank workers, set targets, etc.).

**(b)** *Workers choose actions.* Each worker $i$ picks:
- Effort $e_i$ on each task,
- Help $a_{ij}$ to peers,
- Sabotage $\sigma_{ij}$ against peers (only under tournament),
as best response to the announced wage rule + behavioral rules (1–10 above).

**(c)** *Signals realise.* $s_{ij} = \varepsilon_i g_j(e_{ij}) + \text{help} - \text{sabotage} + \text{noise}_j$.

**(d)** *Team & firm output.* $\bar s_{\text{team}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum s_i$; $V_{\text{firm}} = \sum_i s_i - \sum_i w_i$.

**(e)** *Wages paid.* Contract.wage returns $w_i$. Workers update $\bar w_i, Y_i^{\text{target}}, \mathcal{N}_i$'s belief about $\varepsilon_j$.

## 4. Treatment layer

Assign $T_i \in \{0, 1\}$ (AI access) randomly to a share $\pi$ of workers. AI shifts the technology:

$$g_j(e) \;\to\; g_j^{T=1}(e) = (1 + \alpha_{\text{AI}})\, g_j(e)$$

or equivalently reduces effort cost:

$$c(e) \;\to\; c^{T=1}(e) = (1 - \eta_{\text{AI}})\, c(e)$$

Structural ATE is the parameter $\tau = \alpha_{\text{AI}}$ (or $\eta_{\text{AI}}$).

## 5. Outcome measurement

Compute the composite outcome from the **Quindi Optimal Reward Formula**:

$$R_i \;=\; \boldsymbol{\beta}^{*\top} \mathbf{s}_i \;=\; \beta_3^{*} s_3(i) + \beta_4^{*} s_4(i) + \beta_5^{*} s_5 + \beta_6^{*} s_6(i)$$

Estimate ATE from simulated data:

$$\hat\tau \;=\; \bar R_{T=1} - \bar R_{T=0}$$

**Bias**: $\text{bias} = \hat\tau - \tau$ (accessible because you know $\tau$ inside the simulation).

## 6. Comparison across contracts

Run steps 1–5 for each contract A0–A9, holding population and shocks fixed. Report per contract:

| Metric | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| Aggregate output $\sum s_i$ | Productive efficiency |
| Wage bill $\sum w_i$ | Cost |
| Effort distribution | Worker welfare |
| Wage variance $\mathrm{Var}(w_i)$ | Risk transfer (F4) |
| Cooperation flags $\sum a_{ij}$ | F5 outcome |
| Sabotage flags $\sum \sigma_{ij}$ | Tournament pathology |
| Bunching mass at target | F6 outcome |
| $\text{bias}(\hat\tau)$ | ATE identification quality |

## 7. Robustness sweeps

Grid over key parameters:
- Risk aversion $\rho$: low → high
- Team size $n$: 2, 5, 10, 25 (free-rider strength)
- Peer-network topology: Erdős–Rényi, small-world, scale-free
- Effort-cost curvature $k$
- Noise variance $\sigma^{2}$ (F1 severity)
- Treatment intensity $\pi$ (SUTVA / saturation)

Identify Pareto-dominant contracts and the regions where $\text{bias}(\hat\tau) \to 0$.

---

# Concrete tech stack

**Language**: Python 3.11 + **Mesa 2.x** (agent-based framework).

Alternatives: NetLogo (fast prototyping), Julia + **Agents.jl** (fast + expressive), C++/GAMA (large scale).

**Repo layout**:
```
quindi-abm/
├── agents.py      # Worker class + behavioral rules (1-10)
├── contracts.py   # Plug-in Contract implementations A0-A9
├── network.py     # Peer network construction
├── model.py       # Mesa Model orchestrating one time step
├── simulate.py    # Batch runner over (contract, seed) grid
├── measure.py     # Compute R_i, tau_hat, biases
├── analysis.ipynb # Plots, comparison tables, robustness
└── config.yaml    # Parameters, distributions, treatment specs
```

**Data collection**: Mesa's `DataCollector` logs `(t, agent_id, contract, T_i, e_i, a_ij, sigma_ij, s_i, w_i, R_i)` for every period. Turn into a long panel `pandas.DataFrame`.

**ATE estimation**: regressions on the simulated panel — matches how you'd analyse real Quindi data. Statsmodels / linearmodels.

**Reproducibility**: seed every RNG (numpy, network draw, contract stochastics). Ship a `docker` container.

**Scale target**: $N = 10{,}000$ workers, $T = 500$ periods, 20 contract configurations, 100 seeds — feasible on a single machine overnight.

---

# Literature grounding

| Reference | What it gives the ABM |
|---|---|
| **Neugart & Richiardi (2018)** *Handbook of Computational Economics* | Survey of labor-market ABMs; design patterns |
| **Axtell (1999, 2001)** *AER Papers & Proceedings; ASSA* | Firm-emergence ABM with free-riding — closest ancestor |
| **Fagiolo, Dosi & Gabriele (2004)** *IJME* | Labor-market ABM with heterogeneous workers/firms + search |
| **Bewley (1999)** *Why Wages Don't Fall* | Behavioral micro-foundations (fairness, reciprocity) motivating rules 6–8 |
| **Squazzoni (2014)** | Computational sociology of workplace cooperation |
| **Dawid, Gemkow, Harting, van der Hoog & Neugart (2012)** *EURACE* | Full-scale labor-market ABM within macro model |
| **Gemkow & Neugart (2011)** *Rev Netw Econ* | Endogenous peer network + wage effects |
| **Riccetti, Russo & Gallegati (2015)** *JEIC* | Heterogeneous workers + firms + wage bargaining/posting |
| **Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2005, 2010)** *QJE, REStud* | Empirical calibration targets for rules 4, 5, 8, 10 |
| **Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan (2003)** *JPE* | Calibration target for team-pay cooperation shift |
| **Fehr & Falk (2002)** *EER* | Reciprocity module (rule 7) |
| **Kahneman & Tversky (1979)** *Econometrica* | Loss-aversion module (rule 6) |
| **Camerer et al. (1997)** *QJE* | Field evidence for rule 6 |

## Prior similar attempts — an honest gap statement

No published paper implements **all A1–A9 as swappable modules in one ABM with an ATE identification analysis**. The closest neighbours are:
- Axtell (2001) — firm dynamics with A0/A4 only;
- EURACE-type macro ABMs — many contracts implemented but no per-contract ATE-bias comparison;
- Squazzoni (2014) — cooperation-under-contract simulations without heterogeneous-firm identification.

Building this for Quindi is a genuine contribution.

---

### References

- **Neugart, M. & Richiardi, M. (2018)**. Agent-based models of the labor market. In *Handbook of Computational Economics*, Vol. 4.
- **Axtell, R. (2001)**. The emergence of firms in a population of agents. *SFI Working Paper*; later in various venues.
- **Fagiolo, G., Dosi, G. & Gabriele, R. (2004)**. Matching, bargaining and wage setting in an evolutionary model of labor market. *International Journal of Modern Physics C*, 15, 1–16.
- **Dawid, H., Gemkow, S., Harting, P., van der Hoog, S. & Neugart, M. (2012)**. The EURACE@Unibi model. *Working Paper*.
- **Gemkow, S. & Neugart, M. (2011)**. Referral hiring, endogenous social networks, and inequality: an agent-based analysis. *Journal of Evolutionary Economics*, 21, 703–719.
- **Riccetti, L., Russo, A. & Gallegati, M. (2015)**. An agent based decentralized matching macroeconomic model. *JEIC*, 12(1), 51–75.
- **Bewley, T. (1999)**. *Why Wages Don't Fall During a Recession*. Harvard University Press.
- **Squazzoni, F. (2014)**. *Agent-Based Computational Sociology*. Wiley.
- **Shapiro, C. & Stiglitz, J. (1984)** — rule 1.
- **Alchian & Demsetz (1972); Holmström (1982); Kandel & Lazear (1992)** — rule 2.
- **Holmström & Milgrom (1991)** — rule 3.
- **Gibbons (1987); Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2005)** — rule 4.
- **Chan (1996); Lazear (1989)** — rule 5.
- **Kahneman–Tversky (1979); Camerer–Babcock–Loewenstein–Thaler (1997)** — rule 6.
- **Akerlof (1982); Fehr & Falk (2002)** — rule 7.
- **Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2005, 2010); Mas & Moretti (2009)** — rule 8.
- **Holmström (1982); Gibbons & Murphy (1992)** — rule 9.
- **Hamilton–Nickerson–Owan (2003); Encinosa–Gaynor–Rebitzer (2007)** — rule 10.
- **Mesa (Python)** — https://mesa.readthedocs.io
- **Agents.jl (Julia)** — https://juliadynamics.github.io/Agents.jl

nodes.title: ★ Optimal Quindi Reward Formula
nodes.content:
# Optimal Quindi Reward Formula

## Umbrella frame (Holmström–Milgrom 1987)

> Under CARA + Gaussian noise, the optimal linear contract is $w = \alpha + \beta \cdot s$, where $s$ is a **signal vector**. Piece rates = a specific $(\beta, s)$; tournaments = ranking-based $s$; profit share = team $s$. The design choice is **what signal $s$** you contract on and **whose $s$** (self, peer, team, firm).

## Signal vector for Quindi

Four signals, each targeting a distinct failure family:

| # | Signal | Definition | Whose | Fixes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $s_3$ | Peer-relative combined index (quantity + quality) | $[q_i - \bar q_{\text{peers}}] + \lambda [Q_i - \bar Q_{\text{peers}}]$ | Self vs peers | **F1**, **F2**, **F3** |
| $s_4$ | Cooperation signal | mentoring hits, help-given, knowledge-share flags | Self + peer-reported | **F5**, **F7** |
| $s_5$ | Team output | small-team KPI ($N \approx 5$) | Team | **F5**, **F7** |
| $s_6$ | Subjective manager rating | manager's assessment | Manager | **F1**, **F2**, **F6** |

Definitions:
- $q_i$ = individual throughput (calls closed, tickets resolved),
- $Q_i$ = individual quality (CSAT, error rate, rework),
- $\bar q_{\text{peers}}, \bar Q_{\text{peers}}$ = peer-group means,
- $\lambda > 0$ = relative price of quality vs quantity.

## Contract

$$\boxed{\; w_i \;=\; \alpha \;+\; \beta_3\, s_{3}(i) \;+\; \beta_4\, s_{4}(i) \;+\; \beta_5\, s_{5} \;+\; \beta_6\, s_{6}(i) \;}$$

Unpacked:

$$
w_i \;=\; \underbrace{\alpha}_{\text{floor (F4)}} + \underbrace{\beta_3 \big[(q_i - \bar q_{\text{peers}}) + \lambda (Q_i - \bar Q_{\text{peers}})\big]}_{\text{peer-relative Q+Q, F1/F2/F3}} + \underbrace{\beta_4\, s_{4}(i)}_{\text{cooperation, F5}} + \underbrace{\beta_5\, s_{5}}_{\text{team share, F5/F7}} + \underbrace{\beta_6\, s_{6}(i)}_{\text{subjective, F1/F2/F6}}
$$

## Optimal weight vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{*}$

From Holmström–Milgrom (1991) multitasking:

$$\boxed{\; \boldsymbol{\beta}^{*} \;=\; \big(I + \rho\, C\, \Sigma\big)^{-1}\, \mathbf{g}' \;}$$

where $\boldsymbol{\beta} = (\beta_3, \beta_4, \beta_5, \beta_6)^\top$ and
- $\mathbf{g}' = (\partial V / \partial e_j)_{j\in\{3,4,5,6\}}$ — marginal firm value of effort on each dim,
- $C$ — effort-cost Hessian ($4 \times 4$),
- $\Sigma$ — noise covariance of $(s_3, s_4, s_5, s_6)$,
- $\rho$ — CARA risk aversion of workforce.

**Reading it**:
- $\Sigma_{jj} \uparrow$ (noisier signal) $\Rightarrow \beta_j^{*} \downarrow$: don't pay heavily on noisy signals.
- Off-diagonal $\Sigma_{jk} > 0$ (correlated) $\Rightarrow$ down-weight the noisier of the pair.
- $\rho \uparrow$ (risk-averse) $\Rightarrow$ all $\beta_j^{*} \downarrow$: shift toward fixed pay $\alpha$.

**Balance condition** (no dimension arbitrable):

$$\frac{\beta_j^{*}}{\beta_k^{*}} \;=\; \frac{g_j' / (1 + \rho\,\sigma_j^2\, k_j / g_j'^{\,2})}{g_k' / (1 + \rho\,\sigma_k^2\, k_k / g_k'^{\,2})}$$

## Optimal $\lambda^{*}$

Set $\lambda$ so quantity and quality generate equal marginal firm value:

$$\lambda^{*} \;=\; \frac{\partial V / \partial Q}{\partial V / \partial q}$$

## Estimating parameters from Quindi data

- **$\sigma_j^2$** — residual variance of $s_j$ after netting worker fixed effects.
- **$\rho$** — risk-preference survey OR back out via WTA in current pay.
- **$k_j = c_{jj}''$** — labor-supply elasticity: within-worker effort response to bonus variation.
- **$g_j'$** — firm-level regression $V = \sum_j g_j'\, s_j + \varepsilon$.

With $(\rho, \Sigma, C, \mathbf{g}', \lambda)$ estimated, $\boldsymbol\beta^{*}$ is a closed-form matrix computation.

## What this contract accomplishes

| Failure | Fixed via |
|---|---|
| **F1** measurement | $s_3$ peer-relative (common shock cancelled) + $s_6$ subjective correction |
| **F2** multitasking | Balanced $\boldsymbol\beta$ across all 4 dims, incl. $\lambda$ in $s_3$ |
| **F3** ratchet | $s_3$ peer-indexed, not history-indexed |
| **F4** risk transfer | Floor $\alpha$ + HM-optimal $\|\boldsymbol\beta\|$ |
| **F5**, **F7** cooperation | $s_4$ + $s_5$ directly price the externality (offset the peer-relative sabotage risk of $s_3$) |
| **F6** Goodhart | Multi-dim + subjective override — no single kink to game |
| **A9** selection | Structure attracts cooperative, quality-oriented types ex-ante |

## Implication for the ATE study

Use the composite outcome

$$R_i \;=\; \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top}\, \mathbf{s}_i \;=\; \beta_3^{*} s_{3}(i) + \beta_4^{*} s_{4}(i) + \beta_5^{*} s_{5} + \beta_6^{*} s_{6}(i)$$

$$\hat\tau \;=\; \bar R_{T=1} - \bar R_{T=0}$$

$\hat\tau$ is (i) invariant to intra-worker task reallocation, (ii) cooperation-aware (via $s_4, s_5$), (iii) noise-optimal (via $\Sigma$-weighting), (iv) filters common shocks (via $s_3$'s peer-relative form).

**Cautions**
- **Peer group definition**: if AI treatment is uneven across peers, $s_3$ contaminates. Fix: define peer group at untreated baseline OR use saturation design.
- **SUTVA / spillovers**: $s_5$ team component embeds treatment spillover — use saturation design to identify direct vs spillover effects.

## Bottom line

Four signals $(s_3, s_4, s_5, s_6)$, four weights $(\beta_3, \beta_4, \beta_5, \beta_6)$, plus $\alpha$ and $\lambda$. $R_i = \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top}\mathbf{s}_i$ is Quindi's evaluation index AND the outcome variable of the ATE study.

---

### References

- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1987)**. Aggregation and linearity in the provision of intertemporal incentives. *Econometrica*, 55(2), 303–328 (linear contract).
- **Holmström, B. & Milgrom, P. (1991)**. Multitask principal–agent analyses. *JLEO*, 7(Special), 24–52 (matrix formula).
- **Baker, G. (1992)**. Incentive contracts and performance measurement. *JPE*, 100(3), 598–614 (signal-selection theory).
- **Feltham, G. & Xie, J. (1994)**. Performance measure congruity and diversity. *Accounting Review*, 69(3), 429–453.
- **Holmström, B. (1982)**. Moral hazard in teams. *Bell JE*, 13, 324–340 (peer benchmark / team component).
- **Shleifer, A. (1985)**. A theory of yardstick competition. *RAND JE*, 16(3), 319–327.
- **MacLeod, W. B. (2003)**. Optimal contracting with subjective evaluation. *AER*, 93(1), 216–240 ($s_6$ subjective term).
- **Chetty, R., Friedman, J. & Rockoff, J. (2014)**. Measuring the impacts of teachers. *AER*, 104(9), 2593–2679 (individual value-added under fixed pay — outcome measurement template).

nodes.title: Theory and issue — incentives baseline (moral hazard)
nodes.content:
# The Incentives Literature

The incentives literature — a subset of *contract theory* — asks a single core question:

> **If a worker's effort is unobservable, and pay is independent of output, why would the worker exert any effort at all?**

The answer is: they wouldn't. This is the **moral hazard** problem, and it is the reason every alternative A1–A9 in this graph exists.

## Key contributions

| Author | Contribution |
|---|---|
| **Ross (1973)** | First formulation of the agency problem |
| **Mirrlees (1974, 1976, 1999)** | Formalises moral hazard; conditions for first-best |
| **Holmström (1979)** | Canonical PA model: unobservable effort, noisy signal; sufficient-statistic principle |
| **Grossman & Hart (1983)** | General PA formulation; decomposition into two subproblems |
| **Holmström & Milgrom (1987)** | **Linear contract** under CARA-Gaussian-quadratic — the workhorse |
| **Holmström & Milgrom (1991)** | Multitasking: matrix contract $\boldsymbol\beta$; F2 formalised |
| **Lazear & Rosen (1981)** | Tournaments (A2) |
| **Lazear (1979, 1981)** | Deferred compensation (A5) |
| **Holmström (1982)** | Managerial incentives / career concerns (A6); yardstick fix for F3 |
| **Fama (1980)** | Implicit incentives via labor-market reputation |
| **Shapiro & Stiglitz (1984)** | Efficiency wage (A3) |
| **Baker–Gibbons–Murphy (1994), MacLeod (2003)** | Subjective evaluation (A7); relational contracts |
| **Jensen & Meckling (1976), Hansmann (1996)** | Ownership as residual-claim incentive (A8) |
| **Gibbons (1987), Bandiera–Barankay–Rasul (2005)** | Ratchet effect (F3); field evidence |
| **Lazear (2000)** | Safelite: piece rates → +44% productivity; ½ effort, ½ sorting |
| **Prendergast (1999)** | Survey; documents that empirical piece rates are rare |

---

# The Standard Model — Holmström (1979) / Holmström–Milgrom (1987)

This is the base every alternative modifies.

## Actors and timing

- **Principal** (firm): risk-neutral, maximises expected profit.
- **Agent** (worker): risk-averse, chooses *unobservable* effort $e$.

Timing:
1. Principal offers contract $w(s)$ where $s$ is the observable output signal.
2. Agent accepts / rejects (**Participation Constraint, PC**).
3. Agent chooses $e$ (**Incentive Compatibility, IC**).
4. Nature draws noise $\varepsilon$; signal realises: $s = g(e) + \varepsilon$.
5. Wage $w(s)$ paid; principal's profit is $s - w(s)$.

## Production and preferences

**Firm output**:
$$s = g(e) + \varepsilon, \qquad g' > 0,\; g'' < 0,\; \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$$

**Agent utility** (HM 1987 canonical form, CARA):
$$U(w, e) = -\exp\!\big(-\rho\,[w - c(e)]\big)$$

with risk-aversion $\rho > 0$ and quadratic effort cost $c(e) = \tfrac{1}{2} k e^2$, $k > 0$.

## Principal's problem

$$\max_{w(\cdot),\, e}\; \mathbb{E}[s - w(s)]$$

subject to
- **(PC)** $\mathbb{E}[U(w(s), e)] \geq \bar U$
- **(IC)** $e \in \arg\max_{\tilde e}\; \mathbb{E}[U(w(s), \tilde e)]$

## First-best (effort observable)

Risk-neutral principal fully insures risk-averse agent → **constant wage** $w^{FB}$. Agent chooses socially optimal effort:
$$g'(e^{FB}) = c'(e^{FB})$$

## Second-best (effort unobservable → moral hazard)

Under CARA-Gaussian-quadratic, HM (1987) prove the **optimal contract is linear**:
$$w(s) = \alpha + \beta\, s$$

Optimal slope:
$$\boxed{\; \beta^{*} = \frac{1}{1 + \rho\,\sigma^2\, k / g'(e^{*})^{2}} \;}$$

**Efficiency loss** vs first-best:
$$\Delta = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho\,\sigma^{2}\,(\beta^{*})^{2}$$

## The core tradeoff (risk vs incentive)

- $\sigma^{2} \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; \beta^{*} \downarrow$ — noisier signal → weaker incentive (**F1**).
- $\rho \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; \beta^{*} \downarrow$ — more risk-averse worker → weaker incentive (**F4**).
- $k = c''(e) \uparrow \;\Rightarrow\; \beta^{*} \downarrow$ — steeper effort cost → weaker incentive.

---

# The Issue: "I work and nobody prizes me"

The core moral-hazard punchline. Under **flat wage** $w = w_0$ (no output linkage, $\beta = 0$), the worker solves:
$$\max_{e}\; w_0 - c(e) \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; c'(e^{*}) = 0 \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; e^{*} = 0$$

**Result:** the worker exerts **zero discretionary effort**. Firm output is just $g(0) + \varepsilon$ — pure noise.

This is what the entire incentives literature is designed to fix.

## Two ways out — both cost something

**Route 1: Set $\beta > 0$ (tie pay to output).**

Induces effort — but transfers noise onto the worker (F4 risk transfer), distorts effort across tasks (F2 multitasking), creates ratchet incentive (F3), creates threshold bunching (F6 Goodhart), and kills cooperation (F5).

**Route 2: Set $\beta = 0$ (flat wage) but use another mechanism to make effort matter.**

Each A-alternative implements one such mechanism:

| Alt | Mechanism to induce $e^{*} > 0$ under flat base wage |
|---|---|
| **A2** Tournament | Rank determines a discrete prize; effort raises probability of winning |
| **A3** Efficiency wage | Wage above market clearing + monitoring + dismissal threat |
| **A4** Team pay | Share of team output — internalises cooperation |
| **A5** Deferred comp | Back-loaded wage; shirking forfeits future rent |
| **A6** Career concerns | Market Bayes-updates ability from observed output → future wages |
| **A7** Subjective bonus | Manager's private rating → discretionary bonus |
| **A8** Equity | Residual claim on firm value |

Each layer adds effort inducement while incurring a distortion (see F1–F7 snippets and each A snippet's "How this modifies the base model" section).

## Design question

> Given Quindi's environment (multi-dim tasks, cooperation externality, risk-averse workers, imperfect measurement), *which layer* — or which linear combination — maximises expected productivity net of induced distortions?

The answer is the composite index $R_i$ built in the **Quindi Optimal Reward Formula** snippet.

## For the ATE

Under the pure base model with $\beta = 0$ (before any A-layer):
$$e_i^{*} = 0 \;\;\forall\, i \;\;\Longrightarrow\;\; Y_i = g(0) + \varepsilon_i$$

AI treatment $T_i$ shifts the production function $g \to g_T$ (say, AI makes the same effort more productive, or reduces effort cost $c \to c_T$). Even at $e^{*} = 0$, if AI raises the return-to-effort schedule, the worker will exert positive effort under the new $g_T$. The naïve estimator
$$\hat\tau = \bar Y_{T=1} - \bar Y_{T=0}$$

captures $(g_T - g_0)(0) + $ any induced effort response — the sum, not the pieces.

**Contamination when any $A_j$ is layered on**: treatment interacts with the specific effort mechanism. See each A-snippet for the modified identification.

## Bottom line

- Standard incentives model = Holmström 1979 / HM 1987: unobservable effort + noisy signal + risk-averse agent.
- Flat wage $\Rightarrow e^{*} = 0$: the fundamental moral-hazard problem.
- Six alternatives (A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A7, A8) each induce $e^{*} > 0$ via a distinct mechanism, incurring a distinct distortion.
- The evaluation index $R_i = \boldsymbol\beta^{*\top} \mathbf{s}_i$ (Quindi Optimal Reward Formula) is the ATE outcome variable.

trash.title: A5. Deferred Compensation / Seniority Pay (Lazear 1979, 1981)
trash.content:
**Signal**: tenure. Pay < marginal product early, > marginal product late.

**Solves**
- Bonds worker to firm — being fired for shirking forfeits back-loaded pay.
- Long horizon dampens the ratchet incentive (F3): giving up short-run output for long-run tenure.
- Long horizon dampens Goodhart bunching (F6): quarter-end games matter less if 30-year payoff dominates.
- Solves moral hazard when short-run output isn't measurable but reputation shapes retention.

**Breaks**
- Requires credible commitment from firm not to fire senior workers arbitrarily.
- Creates incentives for mandatory retirement (Lazear 1979).
- Weakens mobility — inefficient if outside options shift.

**Use when**: firm-specific human capital matters, output hard to measure period-by-period, firm has commitment techno

trash.title: A6. Career Concerns / Implicit Incentives (Fama 1980; Holmström 1982)
trash.content:
**Signal**: your *future outside wage*, priced by the labor market from observed output.

**Solves**
- Market averages many noisy signals over time → attacks measurement noise (F1).
- Naturally captures multidimensional output — market cares about overall ability, not one metric (F2).
- Removes the ratchet (F3): market has no incentive to raise your standard if you produce more.
- Continuous market pricing → no threshold to bunch at (F6).

**Breaks**
- Horizon effect: incentive weakens toward retirement (Gibbons–Murphy 1992).
- Effort tilts to visible, market-legible activities → private-value tasks under-provided.
- Requires market observability of individual output.

**Use when**: high-visibility labor markets (CEOs, academics, professional services).
